sources.title: NASA: Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
NPR: Voyager 1 reaches a distance of 1 light-day from Earth
EarthSky: Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth

context:
### SOURCE [1] NASA news release (https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-voyager-1-makes-history-reaching-one-light-day-from-earth/)
NASA's Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026 (about 10:16 UTC). It is the first spacecraft ever to reach that distance. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours: about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). At this distance a command sent from Earth takes about 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, and the reply takes another 24 hours to come back. NASA invited people worldwide to a 'Shine Bright' event, creating a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset.
### SOURCE [2] NPR (https://www.npr.org/2026/11/17/nx-s1-6043115/nasas-voyager-1-spacecraft-reaches-a-distance-of-1-light-day-from-earth)
Voyager 1 reaches one light-day after roughly 49 years in space.
### SOURCE [3] EarthSky (https://earthsky.org/space/voyager-1-1-light-day-from-earth-november-17-18-2026/)
Milestone time 10:16:07 UTC on November 18, 2026. Voyager 2 will not reach one light-day from Earth until about 2035.
### SOURCE [4] NASA Voyager 1 mission page (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/)
Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977. It flew past Jupiter (1979) and Saturn (1980). In August 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, crossing the heliopause. It carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record with sounds and images of Earth. In 1990 it took the 'Pale Blue Dot' photo of Earth from about 6 billion kilometers away. It is the most distant human-made object. Its power comes from radioisotope thermoelectric generators whose output declines every year, so instruments have been switched off over time to save power.
